extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, journalists, and students interested in media freedom and Bolivian politics
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic country-level overview of censorship and media freedom issues in Bolivia, covering film, radio, newspapers, internet, and legal/regulatory developments (e.g., anti-racism law, social media regulation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-racism law
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislation (signed October 8, 2010) that prevents publishing racist media with the stated goal of protecting indigenous communities; critics claim the law defines 'racism' too loosely and could be abused to censor or close media outlets that criticize the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bill was passed despite media protests and without amendments; as of February 2014 no convictions had been recorded under the law, leading many in the Bolivian media to call it a 'dead letter'. Media worried about vague/broad language enabling censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Film censorship and legal risk for filmmakers
rubrics_metrics.description: Filmmakers and documentary makers in Bolivia struggle to make a living, find audiences, and create impactful yet non-offensive work; in extreme cases documentary filmmakers have been arrested for defamation and some filmmakers have been forced to flee the country because of film and censorship laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates both legal risk (defamation prosecutions) and economic pressure that can lead to self-censorship; examples cited include arrests for defamation and forced exile of filmmakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radio ownership concentration and community radio role
rubrics_metrics.description: Around 80 percent of radio stations are controlled by powerful, wealthy families with ties to traditional political groups; independent community stations make up about 4% of total stations and have gained popularity (especially among indigenous communities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ownership concentration limits plurality of voices; community stations serve as important outlets for marginalized communities to express identity and opposition to authoritarianism, and their small share highlights structural barriers to diverse radio media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper economic and legal pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers in Bolivia historically act as a voice of political opposition but face difficulties: low job security, insecure income, little advertising partly due to low literacy, and ongoing legal cases even though attacks on journalists have declined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic constraints and legal uncertainty encourage self-censorship and undermine press independence; journalists demand better working conditions, training, and freedom from government/financial constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet policy stance versus practice
rubrics_metrics.description: In June 2017 Bolivia joined 16 other countries in rejecting a UN Human Rights Commission resolution affirming the right to a free, uncensored internet. However, the Bolivian state reportedly practices little internet censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contrast highlights that formal international positions or votes may not reflect domestic censorship practices; observers should distinguish between rhetorical/legal stances and on-the-ground enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media regulation proposals and criticisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals discussed by then-president Morales to regulate social media (in response to tweets he viewed as bullying or reputation-threatening) were met with strong opposition and ultimately abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opponents argued the government should embrace social media rather than censor it and feared that a proposed law would contain vague and broad language similar to the anti-racism law, creating potential for abuse and chilling effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical state control of media (pre-1982)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to democratization in 1982, the media in Bolivia was strictly controlled by the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This historical context helps explain contemporary media structures, patterns of ownership, and sensitivities around regulation and censorship; legacy effects can persist after formal democratization.
